utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is case number IT-99-36-PT, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, Anna Richterova, assisted by Adele Erasmus, case manager, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. For Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am John Ackerman. I appear here this morning on behalf the Radoslav Brdjanin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. And for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Your microphone was not on, Mr. de Roux, but we note your appearance and with Mr. Pitron. First of all, Mr. Brdjanin, are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And General Talic, you, too? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll commence with the application for provisional release by General Talic. Which of you is to conduct the application? Mr. de Roux, the application for leave to file a reply was lost somewhere between the translation section and the registry, but we've now got it, and we will grant leave. It does deal with at least one matter, new matter raised in the Prosecution's response; but mainly, if I may say so, it is repetitive of what you said in your motion. But if we allow you to file it, it will, I hope, save you from having to deal with it orally during the course of the hearing. And the Prosecution can respond to it orally at the end of the motion. Yes, Mr. de Roux. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, ladies, gentlemen: I have the honour today of requesting the release of General Talic for several reasons which are simple and which I will try to present briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. de Roux, we do have your written submissions in the motion and in the reply, so you need not repeat anything you said there. But if you want to add anything to it, by all means do so. At what stage do you want to call your witness? MR. DE ROUX: I will call the witness in one minute, but -- and we have, of course -- but I want to repeat very briefly, [Interpretation] I would like to repeat what I believe is the very heart of this matter: an arrest, a 17-month detention, and since then, since then, an indictment which your Tribunal at its hearings in the November hearing found so vague that it asked the Prosecution to provide us with a more specific version. Since then, we have not received anything from the Prosecution, and I think that there is a principle which applies in all countries of the world which is the one distinguishing detention from the accusation itself for the Prosecution. For the time being, the Prosecution, in very general terms, very vague ones, that this is not collective responsibility and that we are not judging collective responsibility of a government or a state or a people. You are judging a man. And for this reason, it is appropriate that the indictment contains sufficiently specific facts, and you noted that that was not the case. The Prosecution did not correct these difficulties, and I believe that it is time to ask for application of Article -- Rule 5 of the Rules, your own, your own Rules of Procedure and Evidence, in such a way that faced with this situation, Rule 65, that is, in a trial which seems to have no end - I don't know when this trial is going to take place - General Talic might be able to be released under certain conditions, under conditions which will be explained to you by the witness whom we have called, who is the Minister of the Interior of Republika Srpska, the new Government of Republika Srpska, because elections took place not so long ago. And to hear this witness, I will give the floor to my colleague, Mr. Pitron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Pitron.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, good morning. You have ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll have the witness make the declaration and then you can take him. Sir, would you make the solemn declaration in the document which is being handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Pitron.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, you have in your file several documents, especially guarantees which were provided by the Republika Srpska on 10th of November, 2000, which was signed by Mr. Dodic, the Prime Minister. There is a document entitled conclusions signed by the new Prime Minister, Mr. Ivanic, which is dated 25 January, 2001, which repeats the guarantees one finds in the previous documents, and another document signed by that same Prime Minister on the same date which authorises the Minister of Internal Affairs here to represent -- to speak on behalf of the government to you. You also have two other documents, a declaration by Mr. Bundalo, who was the Minister in the -- of the -- Mr. Bundalo in the government, who gives promises and guarantees in respect of Mr. Momir Talic. Therefore, what I would like to do with you is to ask several questions of the Minister so that he can explain the scope of the guarantees which were provided by the Government of Republika Srpska and how he's going to ensure that these are respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: Mr. Bundalo, would you give us your name, your first name, and your current position.

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: My name is Perica Bundalo. By occupation I'm a graduate lawyer, and since the 12th of January this year, I'm Minister of the Interior in the Government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, could you describe to us exactly what your functions are?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: My function is that I am a Minister in the Government of Republika Srpska, so one of 19 Ministers in the cabinet, and I head the Ministry of Internal Affairs, which has a staff of over 9.000, and I have the competencies provided for by the Law on Internal Affairs, the Law on the Government, and a series of other regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, I would like you to tell the Tribunal whether you know General Talic.

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I do not know General Talic personally, but from the mass media, I am familiar with his name, the functions he performed before the war, during the war, and after the war. According to what I know, I can say that during the war, he was the Commander of the 1st Corps of the army of Republika Srpska. After the war, he was Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. And as a citizen, I know that he enjoys great respect among the people and in the army, and that his arrest caused astonishment, to put it mildly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, I'm referring to the document which was signed when Mr. Ivanic, who was the Prime Minister, on the 25th of January, 2001, and which authorises you to appear as a witness before the Tribunal. Have you seen that document?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the guarantees which were provided by Republika Srpska in respect of General Talic?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I am familiar with the text of the guarantees provided by the former government led by Prime Minister Dodik. I'm also familiar with the confirmation of the guarantees given by the current government, and in that context I wish to say that before a decision was made at a government meeting, the Prime Minister and myself had consultations to see to what extent the Ministry of the Interior is able to assume upon itself the obligations stemming from the wording of the guarantees. I gave assurances to Mr. Ivanic, the Prime Minister, that the Ministry of the Interior is capable fully to comply with all those guarantees and propose that the government should confirm the text of the guarantees that had been previously given.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, I'd like to go back a little bit. You say that you are familiar with the document. Could you tell us whether the document in respect of the guarantees for General Talic was discussed by yourself on the level of the government, and whether it was the subject of a discussion and consensus?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: As I have just said, I had a discussion with the Prime Minister and also with my associates to see whether all the technical and other requirements are available, and I was given assurances by my associates that the Ministry of the Interior, and especially the Public Security Station in Banja Luka, has all the necessary personnel and technical requirements to provide these guarantees; and there was absolute consensus among the government with respect to these guarantees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, I would like to move to a second document which is your own declaration. You know that document. The document on the bottom of the page, is it yours -- the signature on the bottom of the document, is it yours?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: In the document you speak of various measures that could be used to apply the guarantees given by the government. Could you tell us in concrete terms what measures the police can take?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: All the measures required in respect of monitoring and securing the individual provided for by the rules starting from the takeover of General Talic from the Dutch authorities here, his monitoring, his escorting to Republika Srpska, daily monitoring of his movements, preventing any possible contact with witnesses, preventing any possibility of fleeing, reporting regularly to the Tribunal as envisaged by the guarantees, up to bringing him back to this Tribunal when required to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: Could you confirm for us in specific terms that the monitoring that you're able to put in place will prevent General Talic to meet anybody who would not be authorised by the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I can absolutely confirm that, that we are capable of fully meeting the requirements stemming from these guarantees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have concluded for the time being, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bundalo, your government came into power, I think, after the elections last November?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the government of the Republika Srpska is made up of a number of different parties?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It includes a number of members of the SDS party founded by Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. As far as I know, there are ministers from the Party of Democratic Progress to which I believe before I took up my post, there are ministers from the socialist party, and there are ministers which are non-party members, which are not members of any party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question. Are there any members of the government who are members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I am not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that mean there are not?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I think there aren't any.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want to belabour this too long, Mr. Bundalo, but as the Minister of the Interior, don't you know to which party other ministers belong?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I have already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One small matter: You told us at the beginning of your evidence that you discussed with the Prime Minister, Mr. Ivanic, whether the new government would confirm the guarantees given by the old government under Prime Minister Dodik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: We did discuss that so that I could confirm to the Prime Minister whether we have the necessary personnel and technical facilities to confirm those guarantees, and I told the Prime Minister that we do have all that. And that was a precondition for this government to confirm the guarantees provided by the previous government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do I understand from that that you did not consider yourselves bound by any guarantees given by the previous administration?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think what you're saying is, "Prior to that discussion you did not feel bound"; is that what you're asking him?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It would be best to make that clear, I think, in the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Prior to the discussion, your government did not feel bound by the guarantees given by the previous government.

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: This government is a legal government. With respect to this particular question, as all other questions, will be discussed separately, and the government will take upon itself the obligations that it considers it should in each particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I move on, please. Your President, when he was elected, stated that the question of Mr. Sarovic - I hope I pronounce his name correctly - stated that cooperation with this Tribunal, namely, The Hague, was a challenge and a hard question. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I have nothing to add to that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you are of the same opinion, are you, Mr. Bundalo, that cooperation with this Tribunal is a challenge and a hard question?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I think your question goes outside the scope of my presence here and my role in this case, but I must admit that for my government, it is a sensitive question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Has your government put into place any measures to arrest some of the outstanding indicted persons who reside in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but, Mr. President, it seems to me that we are getting outside the scope in which the Minister was invited to comment, so I object to this type of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It is very relevant to the issue which we have to decide, Mr. Pitron, as was made clear by us in the Brdjanin decision. You proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I will repeat the question, Mr. Bundalo. Has your government put into place any measures to arrest outstanding persons against whom indictments have been issued?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I have to say that this government was elected at a session of the People's Assembly on the 12th of January, that it has been taking over its duties in the days that followed - so I actually took up my post on the 26th of January - and we were simply not in a position to undertake any specific moves except those that are part of the daily duties. I also wish to express my personal conviction that this government will address the question of The Hague Tribunal from a different Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 standpoint and in a different way than has been done hitherto. I wish to point out that that is my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So there has been no discussion as yet as to whether or not your government proposes to attempt to arrest any of the outstanding persons, for example, Zeljko Meakic, Momcilo Gruban?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: We simply have not had the time yet to start any discussions along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move then, please, to General Talic himself. It is right, is it not, that your government takes a greater interest in the welfare of General Talic than almost any other person awaiting trial?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way. As far as I have been informed, we have taken upon ourselves certain other guarantees linked to the release of some other detainees in The Hague Tribunal. So there's no special relationship towards General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's not quite right, is it, Mr. Bundalo? General Talic is the only defendant at this -- accused at this Tribunal for whom the Republika Srpska has assumed responsibility for his defence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: That is all that has reached you, but as far as I know, the provision of other guarantees is also ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about guarantees. I'm talking about the responsibility for the instruction or the payment of counsel for his defence.

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I'm not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't know.

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I do not know because that is not part of my competency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the offers which General Talic has made to this Tribunal in respect of guarantee -- personal guarantees that he will return to stand his trial?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of his personal guarantees. I have come here to speak about the guarantees provided by my government and my Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you were not informed of anything that he was personally offering to do.

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I was not informed, though I think that both guarantees should be viewed together, and they should help the Trial Chamber in making a decision about the provisional release of General Talic, taking into consideration his personal guarantees as well as the guarantees of my government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware that an offer has been made that General Talic himself proposes to provide a bail bond; in other words, to put up money?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Has there been any discussion, to your knowledge, whether or not that money will be put up by the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware that there was a guarantee being offered by General Talic that he would not discuss the case in which he is involved with any person other than his counsel?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: That is part of the guarantees that we are providing. Among the other things that we are guaranteeing, we are also guaranteeing that we will make sure that he has no contact with witnesses in his case or any other witnesses in any other case. So that is one of the component points of the guarantees we are offering.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not a witness. The guarantee, the offer, is apparently "any other person."

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I fully agree with you. "Any other person," that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You have offered to have the police, police patrol, to follow him day and night.

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it proposed that this police patrol will prevent him entering houses belonging to other people?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I am quite confident. In our organisation, we have special organisational sectors that are specially trained to provide surveillance and security, and those men under my direct command would be assigned to monitor General Talic and to report to you as the Tribunal periodically as you may require them to do. In other words, they would make sure that he would not be able to contact any other person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At all?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: At all, if such is your requirement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about one gentleman in particular, please. Do you know a gentleman called Bosko Kelecevic?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I am familiar with the name, but I do not know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Isn't he at the moment the chief of intelligence in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, but even if he is, I think that he will soon be replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, you say you're not aware of it, but you say that even if he is, he will soon be replaced. How do you know that if you're not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that is what he did say. He said that he's familiar with the name, but he does not know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can repeat the question. Is he or is he not the chief of intelligence?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're a member of the government, Mr. Bundalo. Who is the chief the intelligence, please?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: The Secret Service does not come under the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and its very name, the Secret Service or Intelligence, makes it clear that very little is known about the composition of that service and even the person heading it. As far as I know, this government that was elected at the last general elections and that took up its duties in the course of January will be making many personnel changes in all segments of the state administration, and from that I conclude that the head of that service will also probably be replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying that the head of the Secret Service and the head thereof is not accountable to the government?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: According to the regulations governing the work of the intelligence service, this service is accountable directly to the president of the state, the president of the Republic, and less so to the prime minister. So let me underline and repeat, to the president of the Republic and partially to the prime minister. He is not accountable to the government as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So any guarantee that you can give this Court would not cover that Secret Service or its heads' activities?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I am giving the guarantees here on behalf of the government of Republika Srpska and on behalf of the Ministry of Internal Affairs which fully stand behind these guarantees and are capable of fully meeting all the requirements of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Two more questions about Mr. Kelecevic. Were you aware that he was the Chief of Staff and Deputy Commander to General Talic?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: As a citizen, I'm aware that he held senior military positions in the previous period. That's all I'm able to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there has been any contact between General Talic and Mr. Kelecevic since the General's arrest?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From what you tell us, you would not be in a position, would you, to know one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I have to remind you that Mr. Talic was arrested 17 months ago, that I have been in this position for 20 days only, that in the period prior to that I was not involved in politics at any high level, nor did I hold any senior positions, so that information of that kind would not be available to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bundalo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you've mentioned two names earlier on, Meakic and Gruban.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Meakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. They are the subject of public indictments, are they?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are they the only ones living in the Republika Srpska who are --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, they're not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- under that term?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I gave examples, Your Honour, I can put the rest that are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Bundalo, are you aware of the name Dusan Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: No, I never heard of that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Indicted in respect of the Omarska and Keraterm camps.

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Predrag Banovic, indicted in respect of the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ranko Cesic, indicted in respect of the Brcko incidents?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Milan and Sredoje Lukic, indicted in respect of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic, indicted in respect of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I know from the media that he has been indicted, but I do not know the man himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Gojko Jokanovic and Radovan Stankovic, indicted in respect of Foca?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And last, Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I know the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Living in Pale?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You do not know that Radovan Karadzic, the ex-Prime Minister of the Republika Srpska, is living in Pale?

utterances.speaker: PERICA BUNDALO
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Pitron.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I think that the questions were complete. I have a rather brief summarising comment I'd like to make, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But first of all, I will let the witness go or do you want him to remain for some reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for giving evidence. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Pitron.

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, I believe the episode that we have just experienced is particularly illustrative of the two conceptions which are in opposition here at this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 Tribunal between the Defence and the Prosecution. We have concrete elements and we have abstract elements. What do we concrete before us? We have an individual who has been in detention for 17 months, against whom there is no structured indictment, and the Tribunal has not failed to point that out at its November hearing when it asked the Prosecutor to be more specific in respect of the charges against our client. We have a file in which most of the witnesses are unknown to us. We don't know their names, and there are parts of their statements which we don't have. What can we do faced with that? First of all, we waited, and I have to say that we waited with confidence, because we did not doubt that the Prosecution would be in a position to support its accusations and that we would be able to defend ourselves. But after 17 months, Your Honours, without a specific indictment, without witnesses whom we know, and 40.000 exhibits in the case file, tens of thousands of which do not concern our client, it seemed to us that we had to come out of the trial and gone into what in France we call a judicial comedy. And on that basis, it seems to us that we were now well-grounded in asking that justice go down its path under conditions that are not inhuman for our client. This means under conditions which would allow him to be free and to be under surveillance. Faced with these concrete elements, what has been presented to you in the few moments which we've just gone through? Once again, the legitimacy of a government democratically elected has been put into question. You have just been told names of several people who have been mentioned whom we do not know and who have nothing to do with our case, nothing at all. Systematically, the guarantees have been denied. These guarantees which were asserted by the Minister of the Interior, who told you in every possible way that he was in a position to ensure that on a daily basis, day and night, General Talic would be under surveillance. Faced with specific elements which all demonstrate a single resolve on our point to keep in detention General Talic, you were presented only with accusations which were not grounded against the assertions of a Minister who was democratically elected. It seems to me that we have conditions today for your Tribunal, through its wisdom, acknowledge that it is not necessary in order for justice to be carried out that the accused be kept in detention. Much more than that. It seems to me that this would be normal, natural - and I hope that my words will be interpreted properly into English - that it would be redounding to the honour of the Tribunal for it to admit that one can consider that one can be a general, a Serbian general, and also to be in good faith and not to try to run away from ones judges. Do I have to recall -- and that's where I'll stop. Do I have to recall that the highest authority of Republika Srpska, spontaneously, did not hesitate to come to this Tribunal without having to have the police look for him, and that is Madam Plavsic. Why? Why, what she -- what she did, would the General not do also? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pitron, I think I am bound to put this to you to have you give what answer you have to it, but you will recall, because you were present, that on the 11th of January, 2000, your client said this: "As far as I know, all the crimes that were done by military personnel in war are tried by military courts or international military courts or the warring states. This is logical and just because the military prosecution and military justice system is there to deal with the army and has the best knowledge of military organisation. I personally feel that justice and law would be satisfied only if I were tried by a military court of law, that is to say, generals who have taken part in the civil wars." What do you want to say about that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. PITRON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember my client having said this. As you have just recalled, Mr. President, that comment was made during one of the first hearings that took place a few months after his being in detention, in a completely different context than the one we are in today. At that time, no guarantee had been requested or even considered. The General was not aware of any of the exhibits in the case file, practically none. With him we hadn't yet had the discussions which we've been having over the past several months, and I think that I can say very sincerely that the measure of the charges against him and this trial, all of this was unknown to him. From January 2000 to January 2001, we have seen 12 months going by, 12 months of incarceration; 12 months of isolation; 12 months of reflection; 12 months during which the authorities of Republika Srpska were asked to provide guarantees; 12 months which, in my opinion, mean that one cannot say today to the General that he said what he said and then hold him -- criticise him for that. One really could ask him directly. That might be the best thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's a matter for you, Mr. Pitron. Now, Ms. Korner, I had not asked you whether you proposed to lead any evidence because you had filed nothing in answer to the Scheduling Order. So what would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't -- we certainly are not calling any evidence. I think that our submissions have been made very clearly in the written response and there's nothing further I wish to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is something in your written response that I would like to ask you about. I realise these things are put into a computer and once it's in a computer it appears to gain some authority which it probably does not deserve, but the case of Neumeister and Austria, to which is referred in all of these cases, once read, simply does not support the assertion made by the Prosecution, and yet it's repeated again and again even after we drew attention to the error.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I noticed, Your Honour, after -- it's not meant to be a defence. It's our error. It was done very speedily. The application arrived just before the Christmas break, and as Your Honour rightly said, a lot of this is cut and pasted from what's ever in the computer. I had overlooked the fact that Your Honour had already made some trenchant remarks about us quoting this case, and as a result of the speed, it went in. It's been the standard response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps somebody will now cure the problem by changing the precedent in the computer. There's nothing further you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the Trial Chamber will reserve its decision on the application for provisional release. Hopefully we'll be able to give it next week. Now, the Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Korner, may I ask you about your justification document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We do have some concern that there seems to be almost a deliberate myopia about this which has to be faced up to. The third -- can I take you to the third protective measures decision, and paragraph 9 where we attempted to explain to you what should be disclosed inter partes in such an application. In the first paragraph of the example we gave, we said that the witness lived in a municipality in relation to which a particular agency had reported that there is presently a high risk of retaliation if it were known that a Bosnian Muslim was to give evidence against a Bosnian Serb. And then after the example had been given, we said the details could then be completed on an ex parte basis which would identify the municipality involved. Now, in your justification document, you ignore that, and you say what we are asking you to do is to reveal to the accused the municipality in which the witness lives, and having set up that straw man, you then proceed to knock it over.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid Your Honour is going to have to direct me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid Your Honour is going to have to direct me to the passages Your Honours has in mind. I received a communication from Mr. Bohlander which was, I understand, copied to Defence counsel, saying that we were not complying with Your Honours' ruling, and it may be that I am missing something, but I thought that we had complied with Your Honours' ruling as far as we were able for the reasons we set out very clearly. One of the difficulties which Your Honours' proposed, as it were, blueprint for how we should deal with this was that by identifying the agency which had dealt with the particular municipality, that taken into junction with the details that remain in the unredacted version could identify the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, let's just take that one by one. The Office of the High Representative has provided a report which you have given us which deals with all - if not all, most - of the municipalities in the Republika Srpska. So there would be no problem in referring to that report because the only argument you put up about naming others is that they deal only with some municipalities. So there would be nothing wrong or there would be nothing that could possibly identify a person by reference to a report of the OHR.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I mean, Your Honour, I'm looking now at the various witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you see, just let me finish what I was saying. I said I would take it bit by bit. In paragraph 6 you deal with what your concerns with are, and you're talking about the premature disclosure of such information. And on page 5 of your response -- your document, you say, "It is the Prosecution's submission that the information which is provided ex parte may be used by these individuals if it were disclosed to identify the witnesses or confirm their identity, and to determine or confirm that the witnesses or their families are or will be returning to a specific location in Republika Srpska." Now, if there's one thing that the example we gave you made clear, that would not be revealed at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, that seems to me to make it fairly clear that if you did what we had asked you, which was to indicate that a particular witness lives in, works in, proposes to return to, or has business connections with a municipality, without identifying it, except to say that it is one of the municipalities of which the OHR has said there are problems for proposed Muslim witnesses. Now, that seems to me to be so simple that your submission that you cannot comply with it could not honestly be held. All you have done in your document, despite everything we have said to you in the third protective measures decision and elsewhere, is to say that each of these witnesses is a person who will be giving direct evidence against the accused, as if to say that was the end of it. You have revealed nothing else. You have not given the Defence any opportunity to apply its mind to whether they object to or accept the protective measures you seek.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I -- I'm sorry, thank you. Can I take Your Honour to the proposed blueprint that Your Honour gave on page 5 of Your Honours' -- of this Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour stated that one of the complaints was that we hadn't even said to which ethnicity the witness belonged, so we dealt with that in all cases. We gave further information about the type of person and the type of evidence that he was anticipated to give. In fact, there were only two, I think, of the witnesses who, it was suggested, would give direct evidence against either defendant. I'm just checking that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I would have thought myself that the most important point you could make in support of your application to delay the disclosure of the identity of the witness is that that witness is in danger. That's what the rule refers to. The Defence has been given no idea of that from what you have put in your document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, because if we specify -- other than -- I see Your Honour's point, that we could have merely referred to the OHR document as a whole without referring to any of the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That is abundantly clear. You couldn't have read it any other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But the actual specification of the actual dangers, Your Honour, we submitted in the ex parte motion, would identify or could identify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The letter that Mr. Bohlander gave you identifies precisely what it is we want to hear from you as to why we should not disclose it to the Defence to enable them to make submissions, and that is that the witness either lives in, goes to work in, intends to return to - or some other expression, I've forgotten what it is - a municipality which has been described by the OHR as presenting difficulties for Muslim witnesses against Serb -- Bosnian Serbs, without identifying the municipality. Now, your response, I understood, was that's all dealt with in the motion. It's not dealt with in the motion. The motion doesn't even begin to grapple with that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If that's what Mr. Bohlander told you, then I have to say that is an inaccurate representation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, what is your response?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said I did not understand, and I said - it may well be me - what it was, what further information Your Honour wanted than that which was contained in the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I do not understand how you could possibly understand it in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it may well be that I have failed to understand with chapter and verse. But if Your Honour's ruling is that what must be added into the justification are the words "and proposes to return to a municipality which is the subject -- which is recorded in the report from OHR," and we have not done that, Your Honour, then I'm sorry, and that can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There seems to be a continual series of apologies which I am becoming very distressed about. The Prosecution has been dealing with this case for over a year now, and I would have expected that you would have a better grip on what this is all about; and this describes it, and I really mean it, a deliberate myopia as to what the issues are. There seems to be a particular problem with this particular Prosecution team and the issue of protective measures which causes you to lose all perspective about this case. Now I think we are entitled to a better assistance than we're getting, and we have to apparently keep drawing your attention to these things. Now, either you do it or we do it, but I think that unless the defendants are given that particular material and are given the opportunity of making submissions in relation to it, then we cannot make a proper decision, which means we will simply order you to disclose the material or the names of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not see that Your Honour -- Your Honour rules that. I do not see how it would assist the Defence to make submissions to say in one sentence, "This witness proposes to return," or whatever, "to a particular municipality which comes within those mentioned in the OHR reports." How does that help them further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Because it would know the basis upon which we may grant you the protective measures you seek. And they have had no opportunity of understanding that, or of making any submissions about it. I don't know what submission they could make. To my own -- from my own point of view, it's a good submission to make, that a person who is living in the area and who would be the subject to possible violence within that area if his or her identity is revealed, I think that's the best point you can make. If you're not going to make that point and you don't want us to consider it, then your application will probably, necessarily, fail.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think one of the difficulties was when we were dealing with this matter is that when you looked at the body of the statement which is wholly unredacted, all that has been redacted - the facts and what happened are there - is the identity, is that by saying a witness proposes to return to a municipality -- let us take, for example, and I'm picking no particular witness, Kotor Varos, thereby the witness comes from Kotor Varos, and it would not be very difficult for any inquiries to be made as to who this witness was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that's not what you've asserted and I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you would have to give us a bit more chapter and verse of that one. Is this not part of some galloping paranoia. It seems to me that you could take this to any length. We have to balance the rights of the accused against the Prosecution. If the Prosecution is dissatisfied with our statement that a witness has to be disclosed, then your answer is you will not call that witness. We are not here to ensure the Prosecution can present the best case. We are here to ensure that the Prosecution presents a case which the accused can fairly meet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I take what Your Honour has just said in stages, please. First of all, that is the point that we did make in the motion, that because of the paperwork that returnees have to fill in, if we say that a witness in the party's motion is intending to return to a particular municipality, not in all cases but in many, and it will identify the witness at this stage. And we say that, Your Honour, that is the point we were making in paragraph 8, page 5 to 6. Can I take that as the first point. The next point that Your Honour accuses - and I'm taking this as a personal attack on me - is of paranoia in respect of witness protection, Your Honour, the situation in the Republika Srpska and other places, Your Honours has seen for yourselves from the reports, is not a policed, civilised country in the sense from the jurisdictions in which Your Honour and I come from. I follow the words of the Statute. I follow the words of the rules --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- which enjoins upon the Prosecution to seek protection for victims and witnesses who may be possibly endangered by the fact that they're coming to give evidence against these accused. Now, if Your Honour will just for a moment let me develop this, these accused are, with the exception of one other trial in this building, as high as it gets. The guarantees, the like which have been made for General Talic, show how importantly the Republika Srpska and others regard the acquittal or, even better, the fact that this case does not come to trial. When we are explaining to witnesses the nature of the men against whom they are being asked to give evidence directly or indirectly, if they are told, "Your identity will be disclosed to the Defence immediately," not just within the time limits before the trial, the response, as Your Honour can imagine, is very often, as we've already explained to Your Honour, that they will not testify. Now, Your Honour, without witnesses testifying, there will be no trials. We are not asking to withhold the names, the identities of the witnesses, in perpetuity. All that our request at the moment is is for delayed disclosure with such time as Your Honour orders, in however many days or months before the trial or the witness is called, those names will be disclosed. For the moment, I am acting no more than in accordance with the Rules and the Statute of this Tribunal. It is a balancing act. It is one which in the end result comes down in favour of the accused so that they do get the names. For the moment, Your Honour, our application is simply that we may delay disclosure for witnesses who have a genuine and supported fear by independent evidence of what may happen to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But the way you have composed your justification document, the accused do not even know that these persons are either living in or may return to or have business with Republika Srpska or, in particular, the municipality nominated by the OHR document as a dangerous one. That's what I am concerned about, that having spent so long explaining to the Prosecution in these various protective measures decisions, you ignore it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did not ignore it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, you have. And I take into account everything you've said, but whatever you've said and you've conceded that you have to apologise for not having given that information. So we have lost all this time to have to explain it to you in words of few syllables so that it finally sinks in. Now I'm sorry to be fairly brutal about it, but this is not the first time that we have had to do this to the Prosecution in this trial. Now, the next thing that I want to raise with you is this: Bearing in mind that this trial, depending upon the results of the United Nations elections, may get under way either in May or June, the amount of time that the defendants are going to have to investigate is rapidly narrowing, and whilst you may talk about days before the trial, depending upon the number of witnesses whose identity will not be revealed at this stage, they are going to require a considerable amount of time to investigate those. And as we said, I think back in the first protective measures decision, it's going to be a lot longer than 30 days, which you had suggested would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just give Your Honour the figures so that Your Honour has some idea of -- there are, in fact -- so far we have disclosed some 88 witnesses in some shape or other. There are of those -- and if I've got this wrong I will be corrected by Ms. Erasmus because she's been dealing with the disclosure. There are only nine witnesses who have had details of their identity redacted. No. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We've dealt with more than nine already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Out of the -- yes. Out of the 88 -- I'm sorry, 87, I beg your pardon, 68 have been disclosed unredacted, except for the current whereabouts, which Your Honour gave leave to redact. Eleven are the subject of protective motions, and -- would Your Honour forgive me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You've still got eight to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And nine are people that we have informed the Defence that we do not intend to call. Your Honour, some of those, and I find some difficulty in sorting it out, as Your Honour does, because of the separate motions, are the subject -- Your Honour has ordered disclosure and they are the subject of an appeal which, at the moment, we've had no notification of at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand that that is not too far away, but I don't know what's going to happen. But I don't want there to be any settling back and waiting for the Appeals Chamber to deal with these matters. We've got to get on with them. And we're sticking by our guns until we are told by the Appeals Chamber that we are wrong. Now, we're 25 entitled to do that; you're not. Now, that leads me to the next matter I want to raise with you for the Status Conference. Back in November of last year, you will remember that I had something to say about the form of the indictment, and you said well, then you would take the blame for your ignorance of the Rules and the rulings, although you did suggest at one stage that you may be lucky enough to have another Trial Chamber hear the case. I did remind you that we're deciding the Rule 72 motion and not some other Trial Chamber, so that what we have said in Krnojelac is what we're going to apply. And I warned you back on the 17th of November to start getting ready -- your indictment ready with the detail in it which the Krnojelac cases require. Now, the decision on the Rule 72 motion is being held up, as we have earlier indicated, until the decision in Celebici on cumulative charging. That is a very small item from the point of view of redrafting an indictment. You either put them in the alternative or you leave them as cumulative charges. So that when this decision is given, which will be at the end of this month because Celebici is coming out on the 20th, you will be given a very short period to file a further amended indictment. So I'm giving you warning that it may be something like two weeks, which means we'll have the indictment, one hopes, a proper indictment, in the middle of March. If this case is due to begin sometime late in May, you will probably be required to disclose the names of these witnesses two months before the trial or at least most of them. There's one or two, I can see, from what you've put in the ex parte material, which will require a slightly later disclosure. So this stand, principled or paranoid, whichever you prefer, is over a very short period of time. Now, there is one other matter that is in the wings, as it were. The President has made an order. He's varied to some extent the order which he made earlier, and in that he has asked you to -- I'm sorry -- he has given you leave to make an application to this Trial Chamber for further protective measures. That has now been filed. Has there been any discussion with the Defence over this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've had no response. We've had no response to this. Neither counsel has raised this with me in any letter. We've had an exchange of letters about other matters. As Your Honour will see, we're effectively asking for consistency in the orders that are made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, yes, but you've also asked us in effect to resolve what you see to be some differences between Trial Chamber III and the President. I thought that we'd made our position fairly clear when we had the task delegated to us by Trial Chamber I as to the way in which we would go about it. But you haven't suggested how we would fit in the problem that appears to have been -- to have arisen between the President and Trial Chamber III with the approach we took upon delegation from Trial Chamber I.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure that it really -- I think we weren't really making a suggestion as such because we merely drew to this Trial Chamber's attention that although Judge Jorda had made an order which appeared to cover the Kovacevic material, so did Judge May, and it wasn't clear because, of course, the new -- the change in the Rules enjoins a judge to consult with the judge of the original Trial Chamber because of the timing. I don't think we were making a suggestion at all. We were submitting to Your Honours that when making the orders, the order should be consistent with the orders that you had already made in the other case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't clear, but now that I have got it, I understand. Very well then. Is there any matter that you want to raise in relation to this Status Conference?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, there isn't. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mr. de Roux or Mr. Pitron, do you want to say anything about what Ms. Korner has said first of all? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you've said very much what the Defence believes in respect of this case, the difficulties in which we find ourselves in order to carry out our task, because for months now we are in this issue -- dealing with this issue of protected witnesses or not protected witnesses. You've been told that 68 names of witnesses have been provided. That is correct, but one must also know the significance of the witness. Among the 68 that were disclosed, there are well-known professors who will give us the history of the Balkans and then witnesses about whom we know nothing. Despite the principle, clearly stated President Jorda, we received a letter from Ms. Korner. That was on last Monday. We haven't yet answered because it was Monday. And I believe that -- well, as regards the fundamental matter here, the fundamental document which is the indictment, the indictment, this is not the third version and we are still waiting for the third version. You say to us that the Tribunal - and we take note of that with pleasure, by the way - that we will begin in May. The trial will begin in May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I said subject to the elections. If one or other or all three of us are not re-elected, of course there will be a completely different situation. But certainly we hope that we will have disposed of the current trial which is ahead of you sometime in May, we hope. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Life is frequently made up of elections and successes in elections. Having said this, I believe that we are still in the same position, Mr. President. I cannot go back to what you very clearly said, but there was last point which you did not take up, which is the issue of exculpatory material. The Prosecutor recently told us, about ten days ago, "Tell me what exculpatory documents you're looking for." I believe that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence state that when there are exculpatory documents in the case filed, the Prosecutor must disclose them to the Defence. We turn the situation around now and we are asked to ask for exhibits that we don't know about because in the -- that are among the Prosecutor's documents. And then they say, "Which are the ones that you want? Which are the exculpatory documents that you want?" That is the third strange way that the Prosecution has of taking this case file. And we would like on this point of exculpatory documents and in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, if there is exculpatory material, if the Prosecutor has such documents, then it should please give them to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, you have told us in the past how you have teams of people upstairs searching through everything in the files. It is your obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I read the letter that was written to both Mr. Ackerman and Mr. de Roux and Mr. Pitron? "As you are aware, the Prosecution is under a continuing obligation under Rule 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence to disclose exculpatory material, evidence. We continue to review the materials for Rule 68 exonerating evidence based on our understanding of what might be exonerating or mitigating. If there is any area or type of material of particular interest to the Defence, please let us know and we will instruct our reviewers to search for this material." Your Honour, contrary to what Mr. de Roux said, he did receive a reply from his partner, Mr. Pitron, in terms which I do not consider were particularly polite, but that is another matter. Your Honour, the situation is we are searching all the material with reviewers for anything that to us seems obviously is Rule 68, exonerating of the charges which are in the indictment. But there may be other matters which the Defence would wish us specifically to search for about which we know nothing because, of course, we do not know what the defence is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's what I was going to say. You can proceed only according to what you understand to be the issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And when there is a pre-trial brief filed by the Defence, you may have to do some more work, but until then, you can only do what you can about what you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's accepted. But over this long period of time, has there been any exculpatory material found?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Found and disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And you are continuing to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Your letter, if I may say so, would have been better expressed simply by saying, "You tell us what issues you see being raised in the trial, and we will keep those in mind when we're looking at the documents."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's one way of putting it. We hoped we were putting it rather more delicately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think the time for delicacy has passed in this case. Very well. Those are the matters on behalf of General Talic. Now, Mr. Ackerman, may I draw your attention to the fact that we have received no response from you to the "justification" document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. That's deliberate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: As long as we understand it. If you don't want to put something on, then we don't wait for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to put anything on with regard to that. This whole issue, in my mind, is getting out of hand and is going to solve itself, it seems to me, before the Prosecution permits the Trial Chamber to solve it just by a matter of the trial starting. In any event, I do have some matters that I want to mention very briefly. I must bring to the Chamber's attention what is now becoming, because of your announcement about an impending trial date, a matter of significant concern. There are documents that we have not been furnished in extraordinary large numbers, that has not been turned over to us, and those documents are probably crucial in terms of our preparation for the trial of this case. One group of those documents are a group of documents that were seized by the Prosecution from the CSB in Banja Luka. I was told at one point that those documents had been scanned, were on CD-ROM, and would be turned over to me within a matter of days. That was back, I think, last August. I was then told that a mistake had been made and that among the documents, they had discovered some that were sensitive which should not be turned over to me, which I strongly objected to, as you can imagine. But then something happened and the process had to be restarted, and I'm given to understand that they started rescanning all the documents in November, and that that process is still going on, and that there may be as many as 25.000 or 30.000 pages of material that we have not ever had a chance to see; and when we do finally get it, it will all be in BSC, not translated, and I'll then have to take the one person that the registry permits me to have and put her on that series of documents, to go through them and bring to my attention any of them that are relevant and useful for my defence of this case. And it could very well be that one of those documents will be relevant and useful to cross-examine the very first witness that the Prosecution would call in the case. I understand, without a great deal of knowledge, that there are also significant other discovery documents that have not yet been furnished to the Defence so that the wealth of material that needs to be gotten around is significant. And because of the way things keep getting delayed - and I won't blame anyone for this, I think a lot of it is just the mechanics of how things get done in the Office of the Prosecutor - but because of these delays I'm real fearful that I will not be able to stand before Your Honours in May or June and tell you that I am ready to try this case, because if I'm -- I've probably looked at less than half of the material that will be supplied to me before this case begins. So I'm becoming extraordinarily concerned about those discovery issues and how those are going to get resolved. And with regard to the witnesses, my records indicate that there are 22 witnesses whose significant information with regard to whom is still outstanding, so we've not really been able to begin any kind of investigation with regard to any of those particular witnesses, so that is outstanding. There's just a great deal in the future before this case can start and that I can feel comfortable saying to Your Honours that I am prepared to try this case on behalf of my client and to do any kind of an adequate job. As Your Honours know, I am also at an additional disadvantage: I'm not permitted to have a co-counsel. The registry won't let me have a co-counsel, so I don't have anybody helping me. I'm basically doing this on my own. I do have some people working in Republika Srpska but not in the sense that a co-counsel would be working on this case. They are more doing investigative work and helping me sort through the documents that have not been translated. So I don't have someone sitting next to me with regard to all these matters like Mr. de Roux and Mr. Pitron because they are not beholden to the registry for the kind of assistance they can get. So that's the position I find myself in, and I just wanted to bring it to the Chamber's attention now rather than later, just to let you know that I'm becoming concerned of that situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In relation to that last matter you raised of co-counsel, as I understand it, the directive has now been changed so that co-counsel can be appointed to work on the preparation for the trial. I think you were part of the group of counsel who persuaded the Plenary to change the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was, yes. I was one of the agitators, and agitated fairly successfully, I think. It has been changed and it's now a situation of whether one would elect to go under that at the pre-trial stage of this case. If I would elect to do so, then it would simply basically divide the number of hours that I'm allotted between me and another lawyer at this stage; it wouldn't give me any particular assistance. I wouldn't get any extra hours, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, Ms. Korner, what about these documents. I remember these CDs and your concern about the return of them, the value being something like $15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The particular collection that Mr. Ackerman refers to was not put on CD because all the collections were being rescanned. It had to take, it had to take its place, I'm afraid, in the queue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Why was it necessary to rescan them? Are you redacting those as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It was necessary to rescan them because a lot of them were completely illegible the way it was done before. That's a complaint that was raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you to ask you about the number of these documents. I remember Mr. Pitron describing the nature of a lot of them, such as traffic problems in Republika Srpska and things. Are these all to establish that the Crisis Staff had some form of control over the affairs of Republika Srpska, or the area that became Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think Mr. Pitron's clearly explained what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. He was just remarking upon their apparent irrelevance, and I'm wondering if you're using a lot of documents to prove a particular matter of control of the Crisis Staff of various activities in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. There are two -- there's been two forms of disclosure, as it were. The first is that we are disclosing in hard-copy form documents on which we intend to rely and documents which fall under Rule 68. But we were asked under the terms of Rule 66(B) by both counsel for full disclosure of the, what are called the Banja Luka collections, that's documents seized from Banja Luka; and as a result of that, these were the ones placed on CD. It includes the documents seized from the headquarters of the 1st Krajina Corps which is of the greatest interest to counsel for General Talic, and within that it includes all the documents. So therefore, there are documents which are clearly not relevant to us or to their defence, but we were asked for full disclosure, and that's why the traffic violations and so forth. With respect to the collection that Mr. Ackerman is concerned about, there are two problems. One is that it isn't yet on disk ready to be disclosed. The second is that, as he rightly said, this, above all collections, contains what we term "sensitive material." We've exchanged correspondence with Mr. Ackerman this week, and we explained what we were talking about when we said "sensitive material." I don't think, as we're in open session, it's helpful to detail it at this stage. Mr. Ackerman objected to us removing documents from the collections which we said were sensitive, and I undertook that when we had removed them, they would be placed before Your Honour before the rules which deal with public interest immunity, or whatever it's called here, so that Your Honour could make the assessment. May I say, as I explained to Mr. Ackerman, it's not that the Prosecution has any desire or intention -- well, desire to withhold, it has no interest, but it feels as a matter of public policy that it would not be right to disclose these particular documents. The offer I've made to Mr. Ackerman is that the documents are here and can be physically searched through by him together with an interpreter. I appreciate that takes up the time. Your Honour, we are doing -- we appreciate that the trial is getting closer, we appreciate this is a collection which is of interest to the accused Brdjanin, and we're making the quickest efforts we can to disclose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is it not usual for the material upon which the Prosecution relies to be translated?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but I think what Mr. -- unless I'm wrong, we've already selected some documents which were disclosed some time ago, but I think Mr. Ackerman wants the whole collection so that he can make a search on CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They're not materials that you propose to rely upon; you're merely giving them as part of the general disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're giving them in response to the request under Rule 66(B).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I just very briefly, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- give you just a short bit of history regarding this series of documents we've just been discussing. When we first began our investigation in Banja Luka, I instructed my investigator to go to places like the municipal building and begin going through documents housed there. We immediately found out the Prosecutor had beaten us to it and had not simply taken copies of documents, but had actually loaded up the official records of three different agencies in Banja Luka and hauled them away. So the officials in Banja Luka do not have any of their own documents any more, unless they've been replied recently, so that made the Prosecutor the sole repository of what we considered fruitful avenue of investigation. And that being the case, I asked Ms. Korner to simply make all those documents available so that we could do the task that we would have done in Banja Luka had we had that opportunity. And therefore, they are not -- they don't fall under those rules that require translation and all those kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They just happen to be substituting for Banja Luka at this point the custody of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you made any representations to the registry about the cost of translating them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no intention to translate any document from those collections, Your Honour, unless I find that it is somehow useful. And so I have a person, who the registry have authorised, to do nothing all day every day but sit there and go through those documents one at a time, which is what's going on. She's been engaged in that process with the original CDs that we were given, and she's been doing that for three months, and she's not anywhere near the end of the first collection, so I suspect at that rate she will finish sometime in 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you may like to draw that to the attention of the registry to see whether you can get some additional assistance, and then if the registry understands that, it is difficult to see how they could refuse a request for additional assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think -- I agree with you. I think I could probably get additional assistance if I needed it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, the only matter outstanding out of all of this, Ms. Korner, is revealing the material that is presently filed only on an ex parte basis. Are we going to leave it to you, or shall we simply go ahead and reveal what we believe you should have revealed?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, we will today add a further addendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I would not myself mind if you put them in the alternative, that they either live there or propose to return there or travel there, without identifying which particular witness falls within each particular category. But it is that fact which is your strongest point in favour of a delayed disclosure, but I think you're going to have to do something along those lines, or we will simply just refuse it. The other part that we raised in that letter was some witnesses had already been threatened. Now, that to me is also a matter which can be revealed without identifying the circumstances of the particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, that is the particular -- that is a particular witness where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think there are two that are --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, there are two. But those two, if we reveal that they were threatened - that's why we put in the ex parte - because of the nature of the report, it will become apparent. That's the one we were being concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps you better tell us on an ex parte basis why you say that because it's not apparent to me why you would not be able simply to say that they had received threats. One of them says they knew a witness in a particular case who had been threatened. Now, it would be pretty hard to identify this witness from that, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's only been one case that would relate to that, and it would be very easy, therefore, to identify the witness if you knew that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you'll have to explain that to us, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I will, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When can you give us that? Because we're not sitting in Krnojelac this coming week, and if we can, we'd like to get all of this out of the way in the time that we're giving the parties there to get on with the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I say Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Filing by 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And then from the -- well, only General Talic has responded, but we would like a very swift reply or, yes, a response, I think, a further response from you in relation to what is disclosed by the Prosecution so we could make an order there. I realise that you are entitled to wait for a version of it in French, but bearing in mind that you probably are able to read it, I do ask you on this occasion to not wait for the French version but get it to us as soon as possible, because we do have - that awful expression - a window of opportunity next week to get this out of the way. Now, is there anything else anybody wants to raise? Well, thank you very much for your assistance. We will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
